plan.title: Push-button melody with an Arduino Uno
plan.summary: Build a button-controlled melody player with a passive piezo buzzer on D8 and a push button on D2. The button connects D2 to ground when pressed; Arduino's internal pull-up resistor keeps the input steady when it is released.
plan.final_result: The finished breadboard has a round passive piezo near rows 10–13 and a square button across the centre gap at rows 20–22. With the sketch loaded and USB power connected, each press plays a short six-note melody, then stops; holding the button does not repeatedly restart it. Release the button before pressing again.
safety: Keep USB and other power disconnected while inserting or changing parts and wires.
Use a low-current passive piezo suitable for direct GPIO drive. An active buzzer or magnetic speaker is not a drop-in substitute.
Do not connect Arduino 5V to the ground rail; this build needs only GND, D8 and D2.

Confirm the button's contact arrangement from its datasheet or an unpowered continuity check: the legs across each occupied row must be permanently connected, while the row-20 and row-22 contacts connect only when pressed.
Do not force components into the breadboard. If the specified button or buzzer cannot reach these holes without stressing its leads, obtain a compatible through-hole version.
Keep the buzzer away from your ears, and place the Arduino on a nonconductive surface.

part_guide.breadboard: The white board with numbered rows holds leads without soldering. Within each row, holes a through e connect together, and holes f through j form a separate connected group.
part_guide.uno: The blue-green Arduino Uno board has a large USB socket and labelled black headers. It reads the button on pin 2 and plays notes through pin 8.
part_guide.piezo: This small round black passive sounder has a positive lead marked +, usually the longer lead. It makes different pitches when Arduino sends tone() signals.
part_guide.button: This square 12 mm push button has four metal legs and a pressable top. Its two internally connected leg pairs are joined only while you press it.
part_guide.ground_supply: This black jumper runs from Arduino GND to the first hole of the ground rail along the top edge. It gives the entire circuit a shared ground connection.
part_guide.piezo_signal: This yellow jumper runs from Arduino pin 8 to the buzzer's positive row. It carries the changing electrical signal that produces the notes.
part_guide.piezo_ground: This black jumper runs from the buzzer's negative row straight to the ground rail along the top edge. It completes the buzzer circuit.
part_guide.button_signal: This green jumper runs from Arduino pin 2 to one button contact. Arduino watches this connection to detect a press.
part_guide.button_ground: This black jumper runs from the button's other contact to the ground rail along the top edge. Pressing the button connects the green signal wire to ground.

steps.title: Position the breadboard
steps.instruction: Place the breadboard flat with its long direction running left to right, row one at the left, and column a above the centre gap. The outer ground rail along the top edge will be the ground connection.
steps.check: A top-down photo shows the full breadboard, with row one at the left and column a on the upper side of the centre gap.

steps.title: Position the Arduino
steps.instruction: Place the unpowered Arduino outside the breadboard, above the ground rail along the top edge, approximately centred between rows ten and twenty. Keep its underside clear of loose metal and leave the breadboard holes accessible.
steps.check: The Arduino is above and separate from the breadboard, near rows ten through twenty, with no USB or power cable attached.

steps.title: Insert the passive piezo buzzer
steps.instruction: Insert the passive piezo buzzer's positive lead, identified by the plus marking and usually the longer leg, into row ten, column e, left of the centre gap. Insert its negative lead into row thirteen, column e, left of the centre gap; gently spread the leads only if needed, without forcing them.
steps.check: The round black piezo sits near rows 10 through 13, with its plus-marked lead entering column e at row 10 and its negative lead entering column e at row 13.

assumptions: No parts were stated as already owned, so all required physical parts are listed as added.
Use the specified 12 x 12 mm four-leg button, not a 6 x 6 mm substitute: the mounting holes and internal contact arrangement differ.
The button's row-20 legs are permanently connected to each other, as are its row-22 legs; pressing connects these two pairs.
The buzzer is a low-current passive piezo element suitable for direct Arduino GPIO drive, not an active buzzer or magnetic speaker.
The buzzer has leads that can be gently formed to fit rows 10 and 13 without stressing the body.
The outer rail above column a is the ground (-) rail along the top edge and is continuous along its length; the other rails are unused.
The USB cable and programming computer are not shown in the breadboard scene.
The Arduino uses measured body dimensions; its visible terminal anchor indices are symbolic.

This black jumper runs from the button's other contact to the ground rail along the top edge. Pressing the button connects the green signal wire to ground.
